HAEMATOLOGICAL__Lymphadenopathy:
Lymphadenopathy is sorted by two axes: localised vs generalised, and reactive vs malignant. Most is reactive — tender, mobile nodes draining a local infection, or generalised nodes from a systemic infection (EBV glandular fever, CMV, HIV, TB, toxoplasmosis) (see viral infections, tuberculosis, HIV). The job is to spot the malignant nodes: hard, fixed, matted, painless, >2 cm and persistent (>6 weeks), often with B symptoms (fever, drenching night sweats, weight loss) — lymphoma and leukaemia (see lymphoma, leukaemia), or metastatic carcinoma. A supraclavicular node is sinister — a left supraclavicular node (Virchow’s / Troisier’s sign) points to an intra-abdominal (gastric) malignancy. Examine all nodal areas plus the liver and spleen, and biopsy a persistent or suspicious node (see splenomegaly).
🚨Some nodes must be biopsied, not watched. A hard, fixed, matted, painless node, one >2 cm or persisting beyond 6 weeks, or any node with B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss), needs an urgent excision / core biopsy for lymphoma (see lymphoma). A supraclavicular node is malignant until proven otherwise — a left supraclavicular (Virchow’s) node suggests gastric / intra-abdominal cancer, a right-sided one thoracic disease (see lung cancer). Generalised lymphadenopathy with hepatosplenomegaly and an abnormal blood count may be leukaemia (see leukaemia). And matted cervical nodes with weight loss and night sweats may be tuberculosis (see tuberculosis) — or lymphoma; the biopsy decides.

HAEMATOLOGICAL__Splenomegaly:
Splenomegaly is graded by size and then by mechanism. A spleen enlarges towards the right iliac fossa, is dull to percussion, has a notch, moves with respiration, and you cannot get above it. Massive splenomegaly (crossing the midline to the RIF) has a short list: chronic myeloid leukaemia, myelofibrosis, and chronic malaria / visceral leishmaniasis (see myeloproliferative disorders, leukaemia, malaria). Moderate / mild splenomegaly is broad: infiltration (leukaemia, lymphoma, myeloproliferative), congestion from portal hypertension (cirrhosis), work hypertrophy from haemolysis (thalassaemia, spherocytosis) or infection (EBV, endocarditis, malaria) (see cirrhosis, thalassaemia). When the liver is also enlarged, work it up as hepatosplenomegaly (see hepatomegaly & splenomegaly); check for lymphadenopathy too (see lymphadenopathy).
🚨Three dangers. A big spleen can rupture — after trauma or spontaneously in an enlarged spleen (EBV, malaria) — causing shock, left-upper-quadrant pain and referred left shoulder-tip pain (Kehr’s sign) → resuscitate and urgent surgery; advise against contact sports in glandular fever. Massive splenomegaly that crosses the midline points to CML or myelofibrosis (or chronic infection) — send a blood film and JAK2 / BCR-ABL (see myeloproliferative disorders). And hypersplenism pools and destroys blood cells — the enlarged spleen can cause anaemia, neutropenia and thrombocytopenia (pancytopenia) with the risk of bleeding and infection. Always look for the underlying malignancy and examine the nodes and liver (see lymphoma).

HAEMATOLOGICAL__Bruising & Bleeding:
Abnormal bruising and bleeding is split by the pattern — and the pattern names the defect. A platelet or vessel problem gives a mucocutaneous pattern: petechiae, purpura, epistaxis, gum bleeding, heavy periods and immediate bleeding from cuts (see petechiae & purpura). A coagulation-factor problem gives a deep pattern: haemarthroses, muscle haematomas and delayed re-bleeding. Then work out the mechanism: thrombocytopenia (ITP, marrow failure / leukaemia, DIC), platelet dysfunction / von Willebrand disease, haemophilia, or an acquired coagulopathy (liver disease, vitamin K deficiency, anticoagulants) — and consider acquired haemophilia A (new spontaneous deep bruising with an isolated raised APTT in an older or postpartum patient) (see thrombocytopenia, haemophilia / VWD, anticoagulation). Screen with FBC + blood film, PT / APTT, fibrinogen. The must-not-miss causes are acute leukaemia, DIC and a major anticoagulant bleed (see leukaemia, DIC).
🚨Three patterns need urgent action. New bruising / bleeding with pallor, fever or recurrent infections — and blasts or pancytopenia on the film — is acute leukaemia / marrow failure → urgent FBC and haematology (see leukaemia). A critically ill patient (sepsis, obstetric emergency, major trauma) who bleeds and clots at once, with low platelets, low fibrinogen, high D-dimer and prolonged clotting, has disseminated intravascular coagulation → treat the cause and support with blood products (see DIC). A major bleed on an anticoagulant (warfarin / DOAC) needs urgent reversal (see anticoagulation). And in a child, bruising inconsistent with the history raises non-accidental injury — consider safeguarding alongside a bleeding-disorder screen.

HAEMATOLOGICAL__Petechiae & Purpura:
Petechiae and purpura are non-blanching — that is the whole point. Press a glass slide over the rash: if it does not blanch, blood has leaked out of the vessels (unlike a blanching erythematous rash). Petechiae are pinpoint (<2 mm), purpura 2 mm–1 cm. The first, reflex question in a febrile, unwell patient is meningococcal sepsis — a non-blanching rash here is a medical emergency → antibiotics now (see meningococcal disease). Otherwise, feel the lesions: non-palpable purpura is a platelet problem (thrombocytopenia — ITP, marrow failure / leukaemia, DIC, TTP) or a vascular one (senile, steroid, scurvy) (see thrombocytopenia, bruising & bleeding); palpable purpura is a vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura, systemic vasculitis, endocarditis) (see vasculitis, paediatric vasculitis). Confirm with an FBC and blood film.
🚨A non-blanching rash in an unwell patient is meningococcal sepsis until proven otherwise. Fever + a spreading purpuric / petechial rash + being systemically unwell (especially a child) demands immediate benzylpenicillin / ceftriaxone and resuscitation — do not wait for investigations (see meningococcal disease). Purpura fulminans (widespread skin necrosis) signals DIC (see DIC). Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) — the pentad of microangiopathic haemolysis, thrombocytopenia, renal impairment, neurological signs and fever (its paediatric counterpart HUS follows E. coli O157 diarrhoea with renal-predominant disease and is largely supportive — plasma exchange is not routine) — needs urgent plasma exchange (see thrombocytopenia). And petechiae with pallor, fever and blasts may be acute leukaemia (see leukaemia).

HAEMATOLOGICAL__Plethora (Polycythaemia):
Plethora is a florid, ruddy, dusky-red complexion. The one question that reorganises everything is: is this a true rise in red-cell mass (erythrocytosis) or not? Check the FBC / haematocrit. A high haematocrit is either primary — polycythaemia vera (a JAK2-driven myeloproliferative disorder with a low EPO, splenomegaly, itch and thrombosis) (see polycythaemia, myeloproliferative disorders) — or secondary, driven by a raised EPO: appropriately in hypoxia (COPD, obstructive sleep apnoea, cyanotic heart disease, altitude, heavy smoking) (see COPD, sleep apnoea), or inappropriately from an EPO-secreting tumour (renal cell carcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma, cerebellar haemangioblastoma) (see renal cell carcinoma). A normal red-cell mass with a high haematocrit is apparent (relative) polycythaemia — dehydration, diuretics, smoking (Gaisböck). And some plethora is not erythrocytosis at all: Cushing’s (see Cushing’s, cushingoid habitus), SVC obstruction, alcohol and rosacea (see rosacea).
🚨A very high haematocrit is a thrombotic emergency. Hyperviscosity from polycythaemia vera drives arterial and venous thrombosis — stroke, myocardial infarction, Budd-Chiari syndrome (hepatic vein thrombosis) — and causes aquagenic pruritus and erythromelalgia; treat with venesection and aspirin ± cytoreduction (see polycythaemia). Superior vena cava obstruction — facial plethora and swelling with distended neck / chest-wall veins and arm oedema, worse on bending forward — is an oncological emergency (usually lung cancer) needing urgent imaging and treatment (see lung cancer). And an EPO-secreting renal or hepatic tumour may hide behind the red cells (see renal cell carcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma).

HAEMATOLOGICAL__Gum Hypertrophy (Leukaem:
Gum hypertrophy is an overgrowth of the gingivae. In the signs-and-symptoms context the reflex worry is leukaemic infiltration — acute myeloid leukaemia, especially the monocytic subtypes (M4 / M5), gives boggy, swollen, bleeding gums with pallor, fever and bruising / petechiae → an urgent FBC and blood film (see leukaemia, petechiae & purpura). But the commonest cause is drug-induced gingival hyperplasia — the classic trio of phenytoin, ciclosporin and calcium-channel blockers (nifedipine, amlodipine) (see drug reactions). Also scurvy (spongy, bleeding gums with a poor diet), pregnancy (hormonal gingivitis and epulis), plaque-related chronic gingivitis, hereditary gingival fibromatosis, and granulomatosis with polyangiitis (“strawberry gums”) (see vasculitis). Look at the whole patient, not just the mouth.
🚨Swollen, bleeding gums with pallor, fever or bruising is leukaemia until proven otherwise. Gingival infiltration by acute myeloid leukaemia comes with marrow failure (anaemia, neutropenic sepsis, thrombocytopenic bleeding) — an urgent FBC, blood film and haematology referral (see leukaemia, anaemia). Bleeding gums can also be the first sign of thrombocytopenia (see thrombocytopenia, bruising & bleeding). And red, granular, friable “strawberry gingivitis” with sinusitis, epistaxis or haematuria is granulomatosis with polyangiitis — a systemic ANCA vasculitis (see vasculitis).

HAEMATOLOGICAL__Koilonychia:
Koilonychia is a spoon-shaped nail — the normal convexity is lost and the nail becomes flat and then concave, so it could hold a drop of water. The classic association is iron-deficiency anaemia, so the sign is really a prompt to answer two questions: is the patient iron-deficient (FBC + ferritin), and if so, why? (see anaemia). The dangerous answer is chronic occult blood loss — in an older adult or a postmenopausal woman, iron deficiency is a colorectal or gastric cancer until endoscopy proves otherwise (see colorectal cancer, gastric cancer). Other causes are menorrhagia (see menstrual disorders), malabsorption (coeliac disease) (see coeliac disease) and a poor diet, with the iron-deficiency triad of koilonychia, angular stomatitis and glossitis (see atrophic glossitis). Not every spoon nail is iron: it is also hereditary, idiopathic, occupational (water / detergents) and physiological in infants.
🚨Iron deficiency in an older adult is a gastrointestinal malignancy until proven otherwise. Unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia (with koilonychia) in a man of any age or a postmenopausal woman warrants upper and lower GI endoscopy to exclude colorectal or gastric cancer (see colorectal cancer, gastric cancer). Iron deficiency with dysphagia, an oesophageal web and glossitis is Plummer-Vinson (Paterson-Brown-Kelly) syndrome — pre-malignant for oesophageal squamous carcinoma (see oesophageal cancer, dysphagia). And beware the mimic: koilonychia can rarely reflect iron overload in haemochromatosis (see haemochromatosis).

HAEMATOLOGICAL__Angular Stomatitis:
Angular stomatitis (angular cheilitis) is red, cracked, fissured inflammation at the corners of the mouth. It sits at a crossroads of three stories. First, nutrition: it is part of the iron-deficiency triad with koilonychia and glossitis, and also follows B-vitamin (B2, B6, B12), folate and zinc deficiency (see anaemia, koilonychia, atrophic glossitis). Second, infection: Candida (± Staphylococcus) thrives where saliva pools at the angles — think denture wearers, and, if recurrent, an immune-lowering state such as diabetes or HIV (see diabetes, HIV). Third, mechanics: ill-fitting dentures, edentulousness and loss of facial height deepen the folds so saliva macerates the skin. Rarer causes include Crohn’s / orofacial granulomatosis and coeliac disease (see IBD, coeliac disease).
🚨Angular stomatitis is a window on the whole patient. As part of the iron-deficiency triad, it carries the same red flag as koilonychia — unexplained iron deficiency in an older adult means occult GI blood loss / malignancy until endoscopy proves otherwise (see anaemia, colorectal cancer). Recurrent or florid candidal angular cheilitis can be the presenting sign of undiagnosed diabetes or immunodeficiency (HIV) — check glucose / HbA1c and consider an HIV test (see diabetes, HIV). HAEMATOLOGICAL__Atrophic Glossitis:
Atrophic glossitis is a smooth, red, sore tongue — the filiform papillae are lost, so the surface looks glazed and “bald”. It is above all a sign of deficiency. The reflex worry is B12 (or folate) deficiency: a beefy-red, sore tongue with macrocytic anaemia and, crucially, neurological signs — so check B12 before replacing folate, since folate alone can precipitate subacute combined degeneration (see anaemia). It is also the third member of the iron-deficiency triad with koilonychia and angular stomatitis (see koilonychia, angular stomatitis), and follows niacin (pellagra), riboflavin and coeliac / malabsorption deficiency (see coeliac disease). Other causes are candidal / infective, Sjögren’s (a dry, sore tongue) (see connective tissue disease) and drugs. The one lesion that must not be called “glossitis” is a persistent localised red / white patch or non-healing ulcer — that is oral cancer until biopsy proves otherwise (see head & neck cancer).
🚨A sore red tongue with neurological signs is B12 deficiency until proven otherwise. Subacute combined degeneration of the cord — paraesthesiae, sensory ataxia, a positive Romberg’s sign and brisk knees with absent ankles — can become irreversible if B12 is not replaced promptly (see anaemia). As part of the iron-deficiency triad, glossitis carries the same red flag as koilonychia: unexplained iron deficiency in an older adult means occult GI malignancy until endoscopy says otherwise (see colorectal cancer). And a persistent solitary red / white patch or an ulcer lasting >3 weeks needs an urgent 2-week-wait referral for oral cancer (see head & neck cancer).
